subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION REPORT- REPORTED U.S. REACTION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION REPORT- REPORTED U.S. REACTION
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the right hon. gentleman taken cognizance of the statement of the state department of the United States, as reported in this morning's Globe and Mail, concerning the proposed restrictions on non-Canadian magazines, and the affirmation by the official that the United States would seek some form of
trade compensation if the Canadian government went through with its plan?
Has the Prime Minister any comment to make on this statement?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION REPORT- REPORTED U.S. REACTION
speechtext:
Yesterday there was a statement by the press representative of the state department to the effect that the reported plan for the disallowance of income tax deductions in respect of advertising in Canadian editions of foreign magazines was of the same general character as the 20 per cent tax formerly imposed by the previous government. All I can say is that there has been no official communication directly received by the government since I set forth the terms of the projected legislation. However, there was an earlier message received by the Canadian government last August.
There is nothing further that I can add. We believe that this legislation is necessary in the interest of the Canadian identity and as an assurance that Canada's destiny will be preserved. As far as the question of compensation and the like are concerned, while believing that this matter comes entirely within our rights and is not merely a commercial question within the terms of GATT, we are naturally prepared, as I said, to listen to the views expressed regarding it though not to depart from the general plan and purport as placed before the house by us. We in Canada believe we have the right to assert the preservation of those things which are Canada's and that our Canadian publishing industry is challenged in such a way that unless action is taken we shall, in the days ahead, be dependent entirely or almost entirely on the viewpoint of another nation, however friendly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION REPORT- REPORTED U.S. REACTION
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. During the intergovernmental discussions which took place recently the communique concerning which was tabled earlier today, were conversations held in connection with the subject mentioned in the question? May I further ask whether or not consultations will be held between Canada and the United States as seems to be indicated in the statement by the official of the United States state department.

subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION REPORT- REPORTED U.S. REACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the progress of the meeting between United States and Canadian ministers that was informally mentioned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ROYAL COMMISSION REPORT- REPORTED U.S. REACTION
speechtext: May I follow up the last part of my question, namely, whether or not consultations will take place with the other government as referred to in the press report upon which I have based my question?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PARTICIPATION IN NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. It is based on a newspaper story by the Canadian press in this morning's Globe and Mail under the heading:
U.S. expects Canada... to join future Inner six talks.
My question is this. Will he advise the house whether the Canadian government is prepared to participate in any new negotiations undertaken by the United States to reduce tariffs with the European common market?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PARTICIPATION IN NEGOTIATIONS WITH U.S.
speechtext: That, of course, is a hypothetical question, Mr. Speaker. It will naturally depend on when this happens and also on the circumstances. I have had occasion to point out that the goals set forth by President Kennedy are identical with those pursued by the government of Canada. We are both seeking an expansion of trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis. After the United States president has obtained the necessary powers from Congress, if he then pursues negotiations with the European economic community and if it is then proposed that the scope of the discussions should be enlarged in order to include other countries, you may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that Canada will be intensely interested. We are ready to play our full part in pursuing the goal that we hold in common.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Rodrigue Bourdages for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Pearson.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government welcomes the test of confidence that is being put to the house in the amendment now under debate introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson). In the time at my disposal today, just 30 minutes, it will be necessary for me to be quite compendious in my treatment of some of the subjects.
I have some comments to make about the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and about issues, both those which he raised and those which he so carefully evaded. Of his speech I will say that in general it was a compound of distortions, errors, half truths, half quotations and selected anti-Canadian quotations.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There was little, if anything, in it that was constructive. If the Liberals have the answers that they claim to have, then certainly they are carefully hiding them. There is no better proof of that than the way in which the Leader of the Opposition, any time anybody asked him a question, sped away from that question as fast as he could. There was nothing new in his speech. Indeed, his speech was most unoriginal. It was a repetition of the same old baseless and empty charges and false accusations. As a performance it was old hat.
It was evident that the Leader of the Opposition was using Hansard, as a convenient vehicle for gathering together in one place a lot of newspaper quotations mostly from partisan, anti-government sources to serve as campaign propaganda in the next election, and he has left Hansard to groan under this dismal burden.
There were many subjects omitted from his speech. After touching ever so deftly, ever so lightly, indeed, almost ignoring some recent events and certainly completely ignoring subjects of very great national importance, and ignoring and misrepresenting the contents of the throne speech, he touched on, I think it is fair to say, three subjects: first, international trade patterns; second, the state of the Canadian economy; and third, he besmirched the image of Canada abroad.
I shall be obliged, because of the time limit, to confine myself largely to the first two of his subjects. In regard to the third, I say only this, that if anyone is astute enough and selective enough he can always find articles in the press abroad that are critical of Canada or Canadian policy. They were there also in the days of the previous government. This is not a new phenomenon. You will find these opinions expressed by people who do not know Canada or Canadian conditions or
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming who sometimes become self appointed authorities on Canada after a week end visit to Ottawa or Toronto or a visit to some Canadian port or city.
But not every Canadian would besmirch his own country by constructing his most important speech for 1962 out of the most careful selection of every adverse comment abroad that he could find, assiduously omitting the many which comment favourably on Canada and Canadian policy and then seeking to exalt his own image of himself by reflecting in a personal way on his distinguished successor, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green).
Sir, if this is the new Pearson let me say, as one who has known the gentleman for many years, that I personally very much prefer the old Pearson.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is obvious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Was Canada's prestige abroad lowered when the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker), at the United Nations a year ago last autumn, made that eloquent and effective plea in the cause of the subjugated peoples of Europe under the heel of the U.S.S.R.; or when the Prime Minister, at the commonwealth prime ministers conference last year, took a firm stand on principles that saved the commonwealth; or when my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, with great patience and persistence has been carrying on an effort at the United Nations on behalf of disarmament and the control of arms and denouncing the way in which the Soviet union has been defeating these efforts?
Did Canada's prestige abroad suffer on these occasions, or did Canada's prestige abroad suffer at those many economic conferences under commonwealth auspices at which Canada took a leading role?
Has Canada's prestige abroad suffered when we see that our relations with the United Kingdom are as close and friendly as ever, notwithstanding the efforts of malevolent persons who misrepresent those relations as being disturbed, and when we have in this way healed the wounds that were inflicted on those relations five years ago by the previous government over the Suez issue?
Did Canada's prestige abroad suffer when our relations with our closest neighbour, the United States, are today as close as ever they have been and are based, I think, on a clearer and better understanding of one another than they ever have been?
For personal reasons I make no comment on the organization for economic co-operation and development. I leave these facts to speak for themselves, and those of us who know him

The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming hope that the Leader of the Opposition will be better able to resist the temptations of the green-eyed monster.
I turn now to the subject of international trade patterns. On this subject the Leader of the Opposition departed far, far from the facts. He has done it before on this question. Therefore I wish to take it a stage at a time and to discuss it as simply and as clearly as I can.
First of all I refer to the European economic community, which finds expression in the European common market. This is an existing fact, a fact of primary importance. The E.E.C. has very important economic goals and very important political goals, the latter being quite often overlooked by some people on this side of the Atlantic. The six countries concerned are moving closer toward these goals and they have declared for closer political integration.
Similarly, they are moving toward a closer integration of their economic policies. They are moving toward a common external tariff, toward the free movement of persons and capital within their borders and toward the erection of a number of institutions.
Our relations with the E.E.C. are, on the political side, very warm and very friendly. All six countries are our allies and we recognize the value of a strong and united western Europe as a bastion of freedom.
On the economic side, the interests that we have in common with the community are enormous. We, along with the United States, have in the post-war years extended aid to these countries and have contributed substantially to their reconstruction and economic revival. We rejoice in their economic comeback.
We look upon the European common market as an enormous and growing market for Canadian exports. We have been taking full advantage, and urging Canadian producers to take full advantage of every opportunity to expand their sales in that quarter. Great success has attended those efforts. Canada's sales to the six countries of the common market have quadrupled in the last 10 years. Our sales to the common market countries are running currently at about half a billion dollars per annum.
Our concern as to the policies of the community are, first of all that they should adopt outward and not inward-looking policies, and second, we have deep concern over their agricultural policy.
The question is sometimes raised: can Canada join the community? The answer, Mr. Speaker, must be no.
The treaty of Rome, which gave rise to this institution, provides clearly that membership is open only to European countries. It is a distinctly European institution. There is


provision for association of what are called associated overseas territories. This category is not applicable to the self governing countries of the commonwealth. It applies to some countries that have been in association with these six countries. We have some examples in northern Africa. So that-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about article 238?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
-there is no provision there for North American countries.
There is an article in the treaty which provides for association, as it is called-not associate membership, but entering into association. Greece, for instance, has become an associate member. It has been made clear by the six that the kind of association which is contemplated there is with less developed countries, and not what we commonly call the exchange of trade advantages. That is not the kind of association which is contemplated. Of course, the community as an institution has been negotiating at GATT. We have been negotiating with them for a year and a half, so that is not to be confused with membership in the association or association in the sense to which I have just referred.
Some Liberals who have been saying that Canada should join the common market- and Mr. Douglas, the leader of the N.D.P. has been openly advocating this-are obviously not acquainted with the subject they purport to discuss. This matter has been touched on by President Kennedy who dealt with the subject in very plain terms when he said: "I do not know what the word 'associated' means in that question". He had been asked whether the U.S. proposed to become "associated" with the common market. Then he added:
I have not heard it proposed the United States should become a member of the common market or associated with the common market in the sense that the word is ordinarily used.
The fact is that Canada, particularly as a country looking for a larger market for the export of its agricultural surpluses, is not the kind of country that the Six would find it suitable to be associated with in the meaning which is contemplated by certain clauses of the treaty as I have indicated. There has been a certain amount of error and confusion on this point and for that reason I thought it well to deal with it now.
I pass, now, to the application of the United Kingdom for membership of the common market. These negotiations are currently proceeding. It becomes, then, a question of what terms can be negotiated. What decision has the government of the United Kingdom taken? It has not taken a decision to enter

the European common market. That is perfectly clear. Hon. members opposite, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in particular, talk as though this was the decision which had been taken. The decision which the United Kingdom government took was to open negotiations, to ascertain whether acceptable terms of entry could be negotiated. That decision was taken at the end of July, not until after Mr. Duncan Sandys had been here in that month and visited other commonwealth countries. The decision with respect to entry will be taken, we have been assured, only at an advanced stage of the negotiations. That stage has not yet been reached. Undoubtedly, the United Kingdom government strongly desires to enter the common market, but not at any price, and Mr. Heath, when he was here-and he is conducting the negotiations for the U.K. government-made that abundantly clear within the last month.
The Leader of the Opposition and some newspapers were saying long ago that the United Kingdom was going into the common market. They were saying this even before the U.K. had decided to negotiate. Their statement has been contradicted by the United Kingdom government itself, and I think they know their own business better than the Leader of the Opposition knows it for them. We are, of course, fully aware of the possibility of the United Kingdom joining the common market and our planning takes this possibility into account. In the present stage, current interest is concentrated on the terms which are under negotiation.
The next question is, what is the meaning for Canada and the commonwealth of the United Kingdom entering the common market? There will, of course, be some pluses and some minuses. We can only consider these in terms of the net result. Obviously, the E.C.M. will become larger and enormously more powerful, both politically and economically. How will it use that power? This is a question which is of vital importance to Canada and to the commonwealth. The policies and attitudes of the various members of the community are not all the same. The question then is, will outward-looking policies prevail? We hope so. Only time will supply the answer to that question.
The importance to Canada of this question can be gauged from the importance to Canada of the United Kingdom market. We sell to that market today approximately $1 billion worth of goods per annum and these exports cover a wide area. They include agricultural products, industrial raw materials and manufactured and semi-manufactured products. There is a great variety in our sales to the United Kingdom, and these sales have been
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming expanding; this is not a static market. Seventy six per cent of all that Canada is selling to the United Kingdom could be affected by the entry of the United Kingdom into the common market, depending upon the terms. This is because these goods enter under the commonwealth preference system and in many cases are guaranteed free entry or free entry with a preference. This is a matter of agreement. Canada has bought and paid for these advantages in the United Kingdom market; it has been a matter of exchange of trading preferences. The United Kingdom market is Canada's leading market abroad for wheat. What of the prospect of a 20 per cent tariff against Canadian wheat if the United Kingdom enters the common market, replacing free entry into the British market as is the case today? That is not all. The countries of the E.E.C. have erected many quantitative restrictions in the course of their agricultural policy. Agricultural protectionism is high in Europe and it takes many diversified forms. If the United Kingdom were to enter the common market without taking steps to protect commonwealth, including Canadian, interests the results could be very grave for Canada and for the commonwealth. Our trade, both in agriculture and industry, could suffer enormous losses and dislocation.
In the course of our discussions with the United Kingdom we have received assurances that they will safeguard the vital interests of the commonwealth or they will not go into the common market. We value those assurances and we appreciate them. We recognize the difficulties which confront the United Kingdom and the heavy responsibilities which Mr. Heath, in particular, bears in these negotiations. We have sought to help him in these tasks.
Here I point the difference between the Liberals and ourselves. They have been trying to push the United Kingdom into the common market. For example, Mr. Walter Gordon of Toronto has been saying on various occasions that Canada should encourage and support Britain's plea to join the E.C.M. Apparently he is not greatly concerned about the safeguards necessary to protect the interests of Canada and the other commonwealth countries the importance of which is recognized by the United Kingdom government itself following our discussions at commonwealth conferences and in bilateral talks.
We can trace this attitude on the part of the opposition to the historic Liberal opposition to the commonwealth preference system and, indeed, going further, to the indifference that the Liberal party has shown in the past to the commonwealth as an institution. They

The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming have shown it often in relation to the commonwealth preference system, and in the blithe way in which they would, apparently, throw away the advantages which Canada enjoys in the British market. They reveal themselves as oblivious to the interests of Canadian farmers, Canadian workers and Canadian producers.
Two days ago the Leader of the Opposition said we had been remiss in not selecting priorities. Do hon. members realize what that means? He said we were remiss because we had not come forward and made proposals for the sacrifice of Canadian interests or producers on the altar of entry into the common market. His idea is that Canadian industries, including agriculture-because agriculture has an enormous stake in these negotiations-should line up on the right, as it were, and step forward for extermination. The Canadian government has not regarded it as its responsibility to sacrifice Canadian interests. We have considered it our responsibility to have due regard for Canadian interests in the larger context of seeking those measures which will strengthen the economy of and good relations within the whole free world.
The importance of these economic factors in maintaining the commonwealth has been misunderstood and underestimated by hon. members opposite. I wish they had been at the Accra meeting to hear the representatives of the commonwealth countries there. Country after country pointed out the importance to them of the maintenance of these commonwealth trade arrangements. Indeed, a representative of one of the leading countries said there, "If you do away with our trade preference, my people will ask what is the use of belonging any longer to the commonwealth?"

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Was that the representative of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No. Some of the newer countries of the commonwealth have not the same background as we have. This fact has been misrepresented and distorted by hon. members opposite but it is a plain fact readily recognized by all who are up to date in their knowledge of the commonwealth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Such as the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I come now to the
question of commonwealth views. The concern that we have expressed is shared by all of the commonwealth countries, and all of the commonwealth countries spoke unanimously on this subject at Accra and elewhere. The misrepresentation of what happened at Accra has been enormous. It has been said

that Canada led a ganging up on the United Kingdom. Nothing could be further from the truth. That statement was published by the nephew of the Leader of the Opposition. It is not a true statement. There was not any ganging up. It is a bad picture to draw of the United Kingdom as if it were not able to look after itself at a meeting of the commonwealth countries where we always meet as friends. When hon. gentlemen opposite take the position that was taken, they are attacking the position of the whole commonwealth, because it was an unanimous expression of concern. And so, Mr. Speaker, there is no right to select Canada as a whipping boy for those who disapprove of a position taken by the entire commonwealth including Canada.
I am pressed here for time, but let me say this. We have always recognized that entry into E.E.C. is a decision which the United Kingdom will take and the United Kingdom alone. We have been concerned for the interests of Canada and the commonwealth, and we have properly, frankly and amicably expressed that concern and the grounds for it at these meetings, as was our duty. The course that we have taken has, in fact, greatly strengthened the hands of the United Kingdom in these present negotiations, the Leader of the Opposition to the contrary notwithstanding.
We are assisting the United Kingdom in these negotiations with all required information in relation to Canadian trade. Those negotiations are about to enter a new phase. There have been discussions at Brussels hitherto carried on by our very distinguished ambassador there, Mr. Sydney D. Pierce. I do not like the way in which hon. members opposite seem to downgrade a very eminent Canadian representative there in the person of Mr. Pierce. But because the negotiations are about to enter a new phase we have arranged to send over a strong team of trade experts to Brussels to be available there at all times for constant consultation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not bureaucrats?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
These negotiations are of vital importance to Canada, and Canada and other commonwealth countries are not parties to the negotiations. Therefore, consultation is of the highest importance. That has been recognized in our talks with Mr. Heath. I have no apology to make for having renewed the request of the Canadian government addressed to the government of the United Kingdom for a copy of his Paris speech of October 10 which was of such vital importance to all of the commonwealth countries. When we received a copy of that

speech we were delighted with it and had the opportunity of congratulating Mr. Heath and expressing our appreciation to him of the full contents of that speech when we had our recent meeting with him. I invite hon. members to read what was said in the communique issued following the talks with Mr. Heath.
Mr. Speaker, there has been the grossest kind of misrepresentation of the position taken by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and myself, at Accra. The discussion there and in our other meetings, whether in London or Ottawa, has always been frank. Views have been expressed in friendly terms. There have been no bitter speeches. Some newspapers have been saying there have been, but their statements are just fairy tales. There is no news in good relations between Canada and the United Kingdom, but if someone can imagine that there is some disturbance of relations, that makes news.
1 do not accept the statements of the Leader of the Opposition in this matter. He was not at Accra, and no newspaperman was inside that conference. But I will accept the statements made by British ministers since the Accra meeting.
One of the leading British ministers at that *conference was Mr. Reginald Maudling, then the president of the board of trade. Mr. Maudling was in Canada a fortnight later and was asked about this. At page 9056 of Hansard *of September 28, 1961, I gave the full text of the Canadian Press dispatch on a statement he then made but at this time I shall quote just one paragraph from it:
He-
That refers to Mr. Maudling; and remember, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Maudling was a veteran of all these commonwealth economic conferences where the subject had been discussed. I continue:
He described the recent meeting of commonwealth ministers at Accra, Ghana, as "the best discussion we ever had". He didn't agree with all that was said but he considered that everything said was reasonable.
That statement was made by Mr. Maudling who was present at Accra.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would you expect him to say anything else?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In the face of the blatant nonsense uttered by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and other hon. gentlemen opposite, here is what was said by Lord Amory, the British high commissioner to Canada, a former chancellor of the exchequer. This statement was made just two days ago on his arrival in British Columbia.
The Address-Hon. D. M. Fleming

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why is the minister so exercised?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The minister is exercised about the untruths uttered by hon. members opposite who utter untruths because they think they will help them back into power and I detest their actions in this regard.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The minister is calling everyone a liar these days.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
These are the words of Lord Amory according to a Canadian Press dispatch dated January 22:
Lord Amory said there is no resentment in Britain about Canada's early reaction to proposed British membership in the six nation trading bloc. "Canada was fully justified in putting any reservations she had fully before the government of the United Kingdom," he said.
Those are the words of Lord Amory. But that is not all. Let me read from Lord Amory's speech to the Canadian Manufacturers Association in Toronto, November 22, 1961. Here are some of the comments he made:
-we in Britain do understand the anxieties expressed by your government-
Speaking of the Canadian government.
-about the possible consequences upon Canadian trade and the commonwealth if we enter the European common market.
Nor have we any reason to resent the forthright way Canadian ministers have voiced these anxieties.
It is right and healthy that on such occasions we should speak frankly to one another, and there is no reason whatever why doing so should impair our friendship or our confidence in one another. I am sure that it is not going to do either in this case. Personal relations between British and Canadian ministers are close, friendly and cordial. And though we each have our own ideas we agree that in a matter of this kind it is impossible to be sure how things will in fact turn out or what their effects will be in this rapidly changing world.
Speaking of the anxieties expressed by the commonwealth countries he went on to say:
Those anxieties are not vague apprehensions without substance.
And further:
We understand very well Canadian anxieties about trade in the various categories of importance to Canada in which there is at present free or preferential entry to Britain-foodstuffs and notably wheat, raw materials such as aluminium and timber, and manufactured goods.
Mr. Speaker, I will accept those statements as accurate statements as to what has been the tenor of the discussions between Canada and the United Kingdom in relation to the United Kingdom application to join the common market, but I will not accept the untruths and distortions that have emanated from the opposition on this subject and, not least of all, those from the Leader of the Opposition that we heard on Monday last.
What of our trade relations with the United States? No new initiative or wider approach

The Address-Mr. Godin would be possible today without participation of the United States having regard to the extent of its interests.
President Kennedy's announcement of a few days ago has been received with the keenest interest by the Canadian government. We have expressed our policy in virtually identical terms. We recognize that his initiative is in the very early stages. His message to congress on the subject is, I believe, expected today or tomorrow. His proposal will then have to run the gamut of congress. It is estimated it will take at the very least six months before congress can act on any such legislation.
We would not wish to prejudice, by what might be considered in some quarters as foreign intrusion, the course that that legislation may follow in congress or the consideration that may be given to it there. It is clear that the United States are pursuing the same goal of seeking an expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis as we are. The means is not free trade, but freer trade. This is not to be confused with joining the common market.
President Kennedy was quite clear on this when he said recently:
I am not proposing, nor is it either necessary or desirable, that we join the common market, alter our concepts of political sovereignty, establish a 'rich man's' trading community, abandon our traditional most-favoured-nations policy, create an Atlantic free trade area, or impair in any way our close economic ties with Canada, Japan and the rest of the free world.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that these words apply with even greater force to Canada's situation. Like the United States, our trade and economic interests are far flung; only we depend relatively much more on foreign trade than does the United States. Just as our southern neighbour has political interests all over the world so our own political interests are very wide, embracing many areas and countries. We have a European heritage and we are a member of the Atlantic community but we also value our membership in the commonwealth, we are a country of North America, we have close relations with the United States, and we have developed increasing trade bonds with third countries such as Japan.

speechtext:
It is an
honour for me, Mr. Speaker, and for the people of Nickel Belt that again this year I should be given the opportunity to join my colleagues in this traditional debate on the speech from the throne. I should like to do as my colleagues on both sides of the house have done and congratulate the seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kingsway) who accomplished his task very well and was appar-
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton).)

ently so short and sweet in congratulating the government.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages), who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and to the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), who has been appointed Deputy Speaker.
I must not forget to congratulate the hon. member who has now become Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. I have to remind him of the fact, that, representing, as I do, a constituency where the mining industry is quite important, I will often have to call upon the services of his department, and I will perhaps be one of those who will be paying the closest attention to whatever he does.
(Text):
I am sure the people of Nickel Belt would like me on this occasion to address myself to the general problems that face us in Canada and not necessarily deal with certain details which hon. members undoubtedly will have the opportunity to discuss under various circumstances during the session. The backbenchers have been greatly helped in this debate, of course, in this way. On the first day we had the occasion to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and also I must admit, we had the opportunity of listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself, who spoke in rebuttal. As has been mentioned, this may be an election year, and therefore the record of the government is undoubtedly a matter for discussion. Notwithstanding what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) believes the Leader of the Opposition, with evidence in hand has indicated to the people of Canada the shortcomings of this government, as a member of the opposition I am certainly proud of the information given on Monday last by the Leader of the Opposition concerning the grave problems in Canada. On the other hand, I must admit that we had occasion to listen to the Prime Minister himself who was called upon to defend himself and the government against the accusations made against him.
The difference between the two speeches was obvious to all members of the house. As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, in the last portion of the first day the Prime Minister, when he was called upon to speak, spent all his time making reference to a document written by Mr. Blakely and purporting to deal with the situation in 1'955 and 1956. Notwithstanding the fair record of the Liberal party at that time we are, of course, prepared to admit that, in the face of the promises of this government and of the Prime Minister, the Liberal party

could not be elected in 1957 and 1958. But surely to goodness the Prime Minister himself does not wish to believe that he can be elected on a worse record.
What was the course of the Prime Minister on the next day? To what purpose did he engage the attention of the house? On the next day we were taken back to 1952 and 1953. It was an example of the old process of diversion. We have problems to discuss and to solve but the Prime Minister took us back to 1952 and 1953. He attacked one Mr. Drury and others. I am told that Mr. Drury has a wonderful record of service in this country. The Prime Minister attacked persons who cannot stand up in this house and defend themselves. Those were the people who were attacked on the second day. That is a type of diversion.
We must recall that the Prime Minister took charge of this government under a theory of diversion. Then it was diversion of trade. We now have diversion of issues. A little later we had a good example of it in the speech of the minister representing Newfoundland. Although the speech was entirely out of order we were diverted into exclusively provincial matters. While we are busy here this week trying to discuss problems facing Canada and to enlighten ourselves with regard to them, we have this kind of diversion.
Then this afternoon we had the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) criticizing the Leader of the Opposition because he, the Leader of the Opposition, had used quotations or information received from people who had something to say in criticism of this government. Then the Minister of Finance himself went on to speak for half an hour using all the quotations he could possibly locate in order to excuse his government and possibly to improve his position. Is that not a diversion from the problems with which we are faced? Let us deal with the problems themselves and not try to divert the discussion into other channels.
If the attempt to divert the discussion in this house fails, resort is had to the old routine of saying that the opposition is a party of doom and gloom. It is no such thing. A loyal opposition is an integral part of our parliamentary system and we appreciate it in that way; it should be so appreciated at all times and not just when the Conservatives are in opposition. It should be appreciated whenever the Canadian parliament sits.
Is the Prime Minister going back to the theory of Mr. Khrushchev, namely complete imperialism? A few months ago we all received reports of the praesidium meeting in Moscow when Mr. Khrushchev had occasion to deliver a speech which was possibly similar to the one we heard last week. As we find from reading the reports of it, nobody was
The Address-Mr. Godin allowed to object. In those reports we have seen absolutely no objection. Is that the type of Canadian parliament our Prime Minister wants? Do the members in this house recognize the Prime Minister who says he wishes to stand for the best traditions of this parliament? What type of tradition are we upholding if we are trying to muzzle the opposition which has a purpose and a function? I realize, of course, that as the Conservatives were in the opposition for so long a period, the Canadian position may not be affected. But nevertheless I believe we should have this respect.
Before I go on to speak about economic matters I should not like the members of the New Democratic party to think that I am forgetting them. Of course, it is rather hard to know what these initials mean, as we hear so many versions. For instance, just the other day I heard Mr. Douglas, the new leader of the N.D.P., referred to as the newest displaced politician. He was apparently so well displaced that even the person who was trying to become his successor could not fill his shoes. More recently I have heard people refer to the N.D.P. as the new demolition party. There may be some truth in this reference. If they are trying to demolish anything, it may be the party itself. We have read this in the papers. I think it is time that someone stepped up to protect the right to vote of the Canadian people. Certainly this party will demolish something if from now on the workers of this country cannot vote as they wish according to their choice but rather must ask someone else in what manner they should vote.
There is no doubt that we are facing an election year unless the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is prepared to imitate in every respect the action of Lord Bennett some 30 years ago when he stayed in office for the full five year stretch. Undoubtedly everyone recognizes that an election should normally take place this year. If the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and other speakers on the government side are right, the present administration must be a great success and I think it is only proper and fair that members of the House of Commons should demand an election this year.
Furthermore, we must demand a proper accounting, something which will satisfy the Canadian people so that when they go to the polls they will know with certainty the problems with which the country is faced. I say that an election should take place but I also say at once that an accounting is necessary. Immediately upon the conclusion of this debate, why could not the Minister

The Address-Mr. Godin of Finance present his budget? That is possible, and certainly in that way the Canadian people could be enlightened.
I have read comments on the speech from the throne. There is not too much to be found in it but I should like to refer the house to a comment I read in a paper that is very friendly to the government, the Globe and Mail of January 20. The editorial commences in this fashion:
There was a general expectation in Canada this week that the speech from the throne, opening what is presumably the last session of the present parliament, would be a resounding election manifesto. It has proved to be nothing of the kind; it would be difficult to imagine anything further from a blast of trumpets. It is, in fact, a curiously thin and inadequate statement from a government which must soon face the voters.
The present situation is a harmful one. In the face of the weakness of the government in expressing itself as to the state of affairs in Canada, people are wondering just what they are heading for. I should like to read another paragraph from the same editorial because it puts the situation quite well.
We shall apparently have to wait until the budget is brought down for an answer-which may be several months. This is hard on the public and still harder on business concerns, which must plan their 1962 programs, without knowing whether they face higher taxes, another bout of inflation, or some radical change in government economic policy. This uncertainty will hardly promote enterprise and expansion.
So far as an accounting is concerned, Mr. Speaker, I think the major emphasis should be on the promises made by the Conservative government, and they are many. There have been discussions about them but I will restrain myself and only refer to a few of them. There is the problem of a balanced budget about which the Minister of Finance, who has just taken his seat, has spoken so often. What is the situation in that regard? We have had deficits ever since this government has been in office. In the last ten years of what they call poor Liberal administration there were not only balanced budgets but surpluses amounting to $2.4 billion. What have we had in the short time that this government has been in office? We have had deficits totalling $2.2 billion. A short period of four years was sufficient to wipe out the surplusses provided this country by a Liberal administration.
There was a promise to lower taxes by about $130 per person. When we review the figures we see that taxes have increased. That is a matter of accounting which should be explained to the house and to the Canadian people. We should be told why this has happened because that was not the promise.
The Canadian people were also told that the government would stop foolish spending and

reduce the cost of government. What do we find now? I should like to refer the house to the figures which hon. members may find in the estimates for 1961-62 and I would ask hon. members to compare them with the total expenditures in 1957, the last year of Liberal administration. We find that in 1957 the estimates totalled $4.8 billion under a Liberal administration. We also find that these people who were going to cut the cost of operating the government are now spending $6.4 billion, an increase of nearly 25 per cent. Is that not a matter of accounting? Should the Canadian people not know why this has occurred. Should these same people who promised a decrease in expenditures not be asked to explain why there has been an increase of this order? Under the Liberal government the Canadian people were accustomed to travelling in a medium-priced car but under the present government they must now afford a Cadillac. I think it is time that we should ask the Canadian people if they wish to travel in a Cadillac under this government or go back to the medium priced car and the costs to which they were accustomed in previous years.

speechtext:
I should also like to thank the whips on both sides of the house for the assistance they have given us in the past in our parliamentary duties, and I extend my hearty congratulations to the mover and seconder of the speech from the throne for a job very well done.
It is not my intention to deal with the major problems facing the country at present. I am prepared to leave those matters to our cabinet ministers, to deal with matters such as our national defence policy, the common market and other problems of that kind, although I have my own definite opinions on them. Instead I shall deal with some of the common problems that affect the common people of the country with whom I have been very closely associated during the last 25 or 30 years.
I am pleased to note that the throne speech foreshadows much new legislation to improve our economy, further, expand our trade abroad, provide more jobs and opportunities for our young people, and assure a greater measure of social security for our senior citizens. Any program proposed to give greater stabilization to Canada's economy must contain strong measures to ensure the stability
156	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. Smith and growth of our farming industry, and I am pleased to note there are proposals in the speech to assist the western farmers in the drought stricken areas by means of acreage payments.
During this time of farm product surpluses in many parts of the world I am pleased to note it is the intention of our government to continue, in an orderly manner, the principle of price stabilization and other measures designed to provide the farmer with a fair share of the national income.
The proposed immediate increase in old age pensions, old age assistance pensions, disability pensions and blind pensions, to be followed by the introduction of a contributory retirement pension for all, will be most welcome news to all Canadians.
The proposal to grant war service allowance to merchant seamen, overseas firemen, Red Cross and other civilian personnel who saw service in a theatre of war, will fulfil a request that was made to the former government on many occasions, but upon which they did not act. Time will not permit me to deal with all the proposals contained in the speech from the throne. However, the more one examines its text the more one is convinced that when the proposals contained in it are put into effect in legislation they will provide another great stimulus to our national economy.
I should like to deal with two segments of our economy that affect the Niagara peninsula in general and more particularly Lincoln county, the riding I have the honour to represent. I refer to our secondary or light industry and our fruit and vegetable growing industry.
I begin my remarks in this connection by congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the members of the cabinet for negotiating last year with Japan voluntary quotas on certain lines of goods being imported from that country in such large quantities that our Canadian industries making goods of the same class or kind were being destroyed.
I regret, however, to note from a press report in the Globe and Mail of January 23 that shipments to Canada of rubber soled canvas shoes and boots exceeded by more than 66 per cent in the first nine months of 1961 the amount that Japan had voluntarily agreed to ship to Canada. If this is a correct report on the manner in which this negotiated agreement is being honoured by Japanese exporters, I think our government should bring the matter to the attention of the Japanese government in very strong terms.
I might say at this point that I do not blame the government of Japan or the people of Japan in matters of this kind. I blame


the importers of Japanese goods, who seem to be most anxious to bring those products into Canada because their margin of profit is much larger than it is on Canadian manufactured goods.
I should like to bring to the attention of this house, and the Minister of Finance in particular, how voluntary quotas on Japanese electronic receiving tubes coming into Canada has helped to provide more jobs for Canadians. I will cite two plants as examples, one in Toronto and one in my own riding.
I paid a visit to the Toronto plant about six months ago, before the quotas went into effect. I found the plant in a depressed condition, with rows of idle machines, employment at a very low level, production at about 20 per cent of the normal capacity of the plant, and the company sustaining a heavy monthly deficit.
I paid a visit to the same plant just prior to Christmas and found a changed condition since quotas had become effective. Employment had increased by over 60 per cent, production had increased by over 60 per cent, and the company was spending $400,000 on plant expansion, research and development to produce new lines of electronic goods not now made in Canada.
I also visited the smaller plant in my own riding owned by an entirely different company and found the same type of progress since quotas were put into effect. The number of employees has risen from 52 to 130. A class of learners is being trained and will be put on the production line as soon as they become skilled in this intricate work.
This on the spot check that I made on conditions in these two plants before and after quotas were put into effect makes it quite certain in my mind that if quotas on electronic tubes had not been negotiated with Japan last year, at least one or perhaps both of these plants would be closed today.
I recommend to the Minister of Finance that he continue his negotiations with low wage countries for the establishment of quotas as a means of protecting the jobs of Canadians against the competition of those countries whose wage rates are a fraction of ours and whose production costs in general are very much lower than ours.
This has also come to my attention, Mr. Speaker. In some cases I believe Canadian manufacturers have reason to complain about the present method of levying federal sales tax and excise tax. I shall cite two cases, one being the manufacture of axes and the other electronic receiving tubes. If a 2i pound axe, which is commonly used in Canada, is made in this country it bears a sales and excise tax of 16 cents. The same

type of axe made in Sweden bears a sales tax and an excise tax of 11 cents. That is a difference of 5 cents, which is very important in these very competitive lines of manufacture.
I also find that a Canadian made electronic receiving tube with a manufacturer's selling price of approximately $1 bears an excise and sales tax of 26 cents, whereas exactly the same type of tube made under United States patent rights in Japan and imported into Canada bears an excise and sales tax of 14.5 cents, a difference of 11.5 cents.
It can readily be seen that this method of assessing for tax purposes places the Canadian manufacturer at a great disadvantage and might very well offset whatever tariff protection there may be on the imported article.
I have found that in some cases goods brought into Canada from low wage countries at a much lower distributor cost price and with a much lower sales and excise tax are sold to Canadian consumers for the same price as goods of the same class or kind made in Canada by Canadian workers.
I have discussed this matter with customs officials and have been advised that in both these cases sales and excise taxes are levied on the following basis: for Canadian manufactured goods, at the manufacturer's selling price to the distributor, and for imported goods, at the value for duty or import broker's purchase price.
I feel this is a matter which should receive some attention and it should not have to be delayed two years waiting for a decision from the tariff board, which apparently is the procedure at the present time. In 1961 some adjustments were made in the levying of excise sales tax on imported electronic tubes, but the tax is still less than that collected on goods of the same class or kind made by Canadian workers in Canadian plants.
I understand some other goods are assessed in a different manner and that tobacco by the pound, either imported or home grown, carries the same level of sales tax and excise tax; so do cigarettes by the pack and playing cards by the pack, besides a number of other articles.
I should like to cite another example of unfairness to a Canadian industry in my riding. This case concerns the manufacture of high test firebrick of a class or kind used in all of Canada's steel plants and refineries. Little or no raw material of the kind required to make this brick is produced in Canada, yet this company is required to pay a duty of 15 per cent on raw material coming into Canada and to compete with brick of the 26207-1-11
The Address-Mr. J. Smith same class or kind entering Canada duty free from countries in Europe which are not too friendly to our Canadian way of life. I think this is a matter which deserves urgent attention.
I regret that Bill No. C-72 to amend the Customs Tariff was defeated in the Senate last year. Had that bill been in effect at the present time I am sure many unfairnesses to our Canadian industries and our Canadian workers could be corrected without the necessity of waiting for long periods of time for decisions by the tariff board.
I should like to speak for a little while about fruit and vegetable growing which is an important industry in my riding and in other parts of the Niagara peninsula. There are approximately 5,000 registered growers in the peninsula. Twenty four plants are engaged in the processing of fruit and vegetables and there are 12 plants which manufacture wines, juices, jams and jellies. Legislation passed by this government during the last three years has given the growers all the protection they have asked for to safeguard them from the dumping of surplus United States crops during the Canadian crop harvesting season. I refer to price stabilization, the assessment of fair value for duty and seasonal tariffs, all of which have done a good job in this regard.
However, the growers have other problems. The surplus pack of canned goods from the United States is always a threat and it has a depressing effect on Canadian market prices for canned goods. The change in the distribution of fruit and vegetables has created marketing problems which have not yet been solved. Small grocery stores and home canning have given way to distribution through the big chain food stores.
The building of new schools, hospitals, roads and the other local improvements which follow housing and industrial development has led to taxes on the farms being increased to a point at which farming is becoming less attractive. I am told that 80 per cent of all the fruit and vegetable processing plants in Ontario is now owned and controlled by United States corporations. The Canadian Horticultural Council is the body which makes representations to the Department of Agriculture on behalf of the fruit and vegetable growers. I hope the council is giving these changing conditions in the fruit growing industry its full consideration.
I have made recommendations to grower organizations and marketing boards suggesting that more facilities are required in the Niagara peninsula for processing and cold storage, particularly for small cold storage units on the farms and increased cold storage

The Address-Mr. J. Smith facilities at the shipping and processing plants. I have also recommended to the processing plants that they should seek some kind of government guaranteed bank loans on canned goods in bond during the canning season when millions of dollars are required in a very short space of time to pay the farmers for the crop and the cost of operating the plant. This, I think, might help to keep some of the smaller independent Canadian processors in business. I have further suggested to the processors and growers that they should seek quotas on imports of canned goods rather than ask for higher tariff protection which besides being difficult to obtain is often not too effective.
I am pleased to be able to say that business in my riding has greatly improved even though we still have problems. There are one thousand fewer unemployed people in the St. Catharines area than there were this time last year. The new subsidy on shipbuilding put into effect by this government last year has greatly helped our two shipbuilding yards, and our automobile parts industries, I am told, are employing more people now than in any previous year.
Water pollution in our rivers and in the great lakes has become a very serious matter especially in the lake Ontario and lake Erie areas. It is my conviction that the regulations passed last year by this government to assist municipalities in the construction of sewage disposal plants and trunk sewers should be extended beyond 1963 in order to encourage municipalities to proceed with major projects which could not be completed by 1963 in time to get the full benefit of the rebate on their loans.
Now I should like to deal briefly with the question of air transportation. During the past years we have seen many changes in rail transportation. Branch lines are being disbanded and passenger services curtailed as a result of which the Niagara peninsula, like other parts of Canada, is required to depend more and more on air transport.
In common with other areas, the Niagara peninsula has great need of improved air transportation for both passenger and package freight. I think the Department of Transport might well review the present regulations for the financing and construction of new runways and the other facilities required for the landing of the types of aircraft now used by industries and feeder air line companies.
I am sure if the Department of Transport undertook the building of necessary facilities, such as longer runways, at regional airports, the congestion at the larger air passenger terminals could be greatly relieved. Industries in the Niagara peninsula that have even

medium sized planes have to keep them at Niagara Falls, New York, or Malton airport, Toronto. I do feel that air transportation has an important part to play in the development of our future economy, and the matter of proper facilities required at regional airports in our industrial areas is becoming more important each year.
I should like to again bring to the attention of the Prime Minister the historical importance of the old town of Niagara, the seat of the first government of Upper Canada. I believe that among the many acts of parliament that were passed there in those colonial days was an act to abolish slavery in Upper Canada. I trust that this part of Canada will not be overlooked when plans are being made for Canada's centennial. I should like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity of speaking at this time, and I hope that I have not overrun my time.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few observations which I should like to make on the speech from the throne. Before I begin, I should like to associate myself with the congratulations that have been tendered to the mover (Mr. Bour-dages) and seconder (Mr. Browne, Vancouver-Kingsway), of the address in reply, and also with the felicitations and good wishes which have been extended to the Deputy Speaker, to our new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Flynn) on their appointments and to the parliamentary secretaries on the occasion of their reappointment.
The more 1 study the speeches from the throne brought down by this government the more they remind me of those fancy Christmas stockings that we admire at Christmas time. They bulge and are attractive and, in some cases, we can get a glimpse of what is inside. There is one difference, of course, because when you get one of those fancy stockings you know you really have whatever is inside of it. This is not always true of speeches from the throne. We know from experience that sometimes the contents have a very unhappy knack of disappearing, sometimes for good, sometimes for several sessions and then sometimes to reappear in quite a different form as did the changes in the Immigration Act which were announced a few days ago by the minister in the form of new regulations.
Well, now we have a new stocking in front of us, stuffed with what appears to be all kinds of good things designed, no doubt, to impress the Canadian people with the wisdom and generosity of this government. I think we can take it for granted that when this

particular stocking was being stuffed the possibility of an election this year was not overlooked. Yesterday or the day before the Prime Minister plucked out a few of those things and held them up so we could get a better view of them. I refer to things like the old age pensions and the pensions for the blind. I am sure we all found them very attractive. It will be a very happy day for Canada when someone can devise a plan which will remove old age pensions completely from party politics.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne had nothing in it to emphasize to the Canadian people that these good things, desirable as they are, must nevertheless be paid for. We, as parliamentarians, are supposed to give leadership to the people. We certainly ought not to lead them into thinking they can get something for nothing. It is quite understandable that the people of Canada do not realize that all these good things have to be paid for because, since this government took office, we have not been doing that. We have not been paying for them out of our own production. Instead, we have been borrowing and paying for them out of the production of others. During the past five years that this government has been in office the apparent generosity of this government has added $2,000 million to our public debt. This seems very strange to me coming as it does from a party and a government that was elected on a specific promise to reduce expenditures.
We can all remember, in 1957, how hon. gentlemen opposite went back and forth across the country decrying the waste and inefficiency of the Liberal party and saying that when they took office they were going to cut down expenditures by $500 million. Indeed, when the expenditures were presented for the year 1956-57 I can remember how the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), who were then sitting in opposition, attacked the Liberal party and castigated the Liberal government because they had allowed expenditures to reach the high level of $4,433 million. Now, four years later, in 1961-62, we have this same group proposing estimated expenditures of $6,415 million and that, Mr. Speaker, is only an estimate. The actual expenditures might very well prove to be much higher. Instead of a reduction of $500 million as was promised, we have an increase of nearly $2,000 million, up 42 per cent. This certainly is one promise the Prime Minister has not kept and, so far as I can see, he is not going to be able to keep it.
The throne speech presents a very glowing account of our economic recovery, and that 26207-1-UJ
The Address-Mr. Carter account has been expanded by speakers from the government benches who have told us that our exports are up, more people are employed than ever before and everything is just wonderful. Well, of course a large part of these exports are accounted for by sales of wheat to China. I realize this is a very difficult question and I have every sympathy with the government that has to make a decision in matters of this kind. The interests and welfare of the farmers and our trading position as a nation are both vitally affected. These are things that cannot be ignored.
But there are other considerations, too, which ought not to be overlooked. In the first place, this raises the question of the motives and values by which our actions are governed. We cannot salve our consciences by saying we are selling this wheat to feed hungry people. There are millions of hungry people in the world waiting to be fed. We are not selling food to them because they are not offering us dollars in return.
Experts who are acquainted with this matter raise a question as to whether the wheat being sold to China is actually reaching the hungry people who need it. There is a great deal of evidence that this wheat is being used as a political weapon, an instrument of coercion, by an unscrupulous government in order to force people to go along with what they want at a time when that particular government is becoming discredited and unpopular. In other words they say, "Go along with us or you do not eat".
In a time of war, trading with the enemy is an act of treason. At the present time, in this twilight zone between peace and war, we are nevertheless engaged in a cold war no less deadly and no less dangerous. The government of China is our implacable foe dedicated to our destruction just as fanatically as is Khrushchev and the Soviet union. We must exercise the greatest care because if, by our sales of wheat, we are bolstering and strengthening an unfriendly or enemy government, it might very well turn out that along with our wheat we might also be selling our freedom.
As the Minister of Finance pointed out earlier today when he was talking about what are the real interests of Canada, surely our paramount interest is to preserve our freedom. That is a matter that must be taken into account in all our relationships with enemy countries.
Someone has made a great deal of the argument that more people are working today than ever before. I really do not see why they do not say that more people are working today than 50 years ago, as it would prove exactly the same thing. There are
160	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Carter more people working today than there were 50 years ago simply because there are more people. That is the only reason that there are more people working today than there were a year ago. The undeniable, irrefutable fact is that, despite this improvement in our economy, our economic growth has lagged and is still lagging far behind our increase in population; and this at a time when our rate of population growth has declined.
If we take the population figure presented by the bureau of statistics for June 1, 1953, 1957, and 1961 we find this situation. In 1953, the population was 14.865 million; in 1957 it was 16.589 million and in 1961 it was 18.168 million. The increase in the four years, the period from 1953 to 1957, is 1.744 million. The increase in the four years from 1957 to 1961 is only 1.579 million. Under normal circumstances the increase from 1957 to 1961 should be considerably greater than that from 1953 to 1957 but in actual fact it is 200,000 less. What a great unemployment problem we would be faced with today if that rate of growth from 1953 to 1957 had been maintained during the period this government has been in office.
Sensible people know that we cannot continue indefinitely going further and further into debt. There is a limit to our borrowing capacity as a nation and there is a limit to the debt burden we can carry as a people. If our economy is to support our present expenditures along with the additional expenditures envisaged in this speech from the throne, our rate of growth must increase considerably over what it is at the present time.
As a Newfoundlander I am naturally most interested in those particular things which the stocking holds for my own province. I wish to thank the government for the reference to the proposed pensions for members of the merchant navy, the forestry units, the firefighters and other groups of this kind who served during the last war. I appreciate the increases in veterans disability pensions and veterans allowances which have already been granted and I welcome this further recognition of the services of those groups which I have just mentioned. I must, however, express some disappointment that the method decided upon in granting these awards is to amend the civilian pensions act rather than the veterans charter. From my own experience I believe that the veterans allowance payments would be far more suitable having regard to the needs of the members of these groups. This decision to amend the civilian pensions act is tantamount to denying these people any status as veterans. A person does not become a veteran just because he puts on a uniform. I refer back to


the gallant exploits of the Jervis Bay. They were unequalled in the history of our naval tradition or in any of our military traditions. Yet these people, if they are entitled to a pension, cannot be recognized as veterans but must get it as civilians. A member of a service can only give his life in the service of his country. That is the supreme sacrifice. When he has done that, he has given everything. I wish to point out to the house the fact that in my own particular riding more members of the merchant navy made the supreme sacrifice in the service of their country than of any other branch of the armed services.
I also welcome the reference to the provision of an east coast ferry service between the mainland and the east coast of Newfoundland. The speech from the throne tells us that the eastern terminal is to be Argentia. Since this is a United States military base I would ask the government to explore the possibility of acquiring access to this terminal without the necessity of having to get permits from the military authorities.
I also welcome the reference to the extension of the period of application of the Farm Improvement Loans Act and of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. No doubt the Farm Improvement Loans Act has been of some use to farmers, but from my experience the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act has been of doubtful value to the fishermen of my province for the very simple reason that the banks have shown themselves to be extremely reluctant to make loans to fishermen.
If the fishermen are to be assisted in the same way that farmers are assisted, some other means must be devised outside of the banking system, and I would recommend that the government consider setting up a fishermen's small loans board to deal with this problem. Fishermen's insurance should also be extended to include nets, gear and other items of equipment which are not now covered and in addition a disaster fund should be set up to protect fishermen against those circumstances and exigencies which sometimes suddenly occur and confront our fishermen as groups and as individuals with disastrous consequences.
We do not think it is too much to ask that our fishermen be accorded the same treatment as is being given to the farmers of our country. It was a great disappointment to all of us that this principle was not followed by the government in assisting our fishermen who are suffering from the catch failure in my province. Hon. members will have learned from press and radio reports that the past year has been a very trying one for our province. Disastrous fires destroyed millions of acres

of valuable timber and brought woods employment to a standstill. On top of that some 12,000 or more of our fishermen suffered a catch failure. In a year of normal catch an inshore fisherman earns on the average a net income of about $650. Out of that he and his family have to try to subsist for the winter and then secure sufficient supplies to enable him to resume his occupation when the season opens in the spring. Under these circumstances it is easy to understand that a reduction in the catch of 20 per cent or even 10 per cent is attended by extreme hardship but when there is a catch failure which ranges from a complete, total blank up to 25 per cent of the normal catch then the circumstances in which our fishermen find themselves are indescribable.
When the farmers suffer a crop failure we come to their assistance by making acreage payments. We are not against that. We have always supported measures providing for acreage payments. We did so last year and the Prime Minister announced that we are going to do so again very soon. But contrast this with the treatment which has been given to our distressed fishermen. When the government finally made up its mind to assist our fishermen at all, this was the scheme that they proposed. First, they agreed to match dollar for dollar provincial road allocations to be spent after October 15 and, in addition, they agreed to grant up to $300,000 on two conditions. The first condition was that the money had to be spent on a winter works program, which it was pointed out was not practicable in the situation in which most of our fishermen found themselves. The second condition was that the provincial government would contribute 25 per cent of the labour costs involved.
Our premier has estimated that this assistance works out to about $20 per fisherman, not for one month but between seasons. On the northeast coast where the catch failure was the worst that means from November to April or perhaps May. It amounts to $20 for 150 days or 13 cents a day per family or roughly 3 cents per head, and that with strings attached. Our premier has termed this treatment shabby. Compared with the treatment that is accorded to other Canadians in similar circumstances, I think he could have said that it is not only shabby but shameful.
There are other matters upon which I had hoped to have time to enlarge. I particularly wanted to say a word about the Atlantic provinces, my interest in whom is second only to my interest in my own province. We all remember the Atlantic resolutions that were framed and advertised so well just prior to the 1957 election. The three most important
The Address-Mr. Carter of these resolutions have still not been implemented, namely, the national development program for the development of the resources of the Atlantic provinces, industrial decentralization and the capital projects program. These are still outstanding and time is running out.
In the meantime the age old disparities between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada still remain. Unemployment is 75 per cent higher than the rest of Canada while income is 40 per cent lower. The unemployment figures released by the government on January 16 emphasized this disparity. In Ontario 4.7 per cent of the work force were unemployed, in the prairie region 5.4 per cent and in the Atlantic region 10.8 per cent.
We shall never cure the economic illnesses or solve the problems of the Atlantic provinces by the piecemeal methods which have been employed up to this time. What we must have is a complete survey of the financial and geographical disabilities under which we suffer. Then we must have measures enacted in this house that will offset these disabilities and put the Atlantic provinces on the same footing as the rest of Canada. We can begin by making a complete survey of the fishing industry and proceed from one industry to another.
I see that my time is almost up so I will conclude by saying that in spite of all the glitter and the fancy wrappings the speech from the throne is not an inspiring document. It ignores completely the main problems with which the country is faced, problems of defence, problems involved in connection with the common market, and others of that nature. It makes no mention of the dangers Canada must face as a member of the free world. It calls forth no challenge. It gives no indication of the firm and wise leadership so sorely needed in these troubled times. Therefore, I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition.
