speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to join with previous speakers in this debate in extending congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also wish to congratulate the Deputy Speaker on his appointment to this important position. It is a distinct honour and well deserved. No doubt he, along with our popular Speaker and chairman, will enjoy the confidence and respect of all members in the house.
I would like to deal with matters pertaining to the welfare and progress of my constituents in Waterloo North, and Canadians generally, under the leadership of our esteemed Prime Minister and his government.
It is gratifying to know that Her Majesty the Queen Mother, along with their Highnesses the Duke of Edinburgh and the Princess Royal, will visit Canada sometime this summer. In 1939 the Queen Mother visited Canada, and her itinerary included my riding of Waterloo North. At that time I was among the amputees who were honoured in being presented to her, and I hope that their visit this year may be a most pleasant one. The visit of the Queen Mother reminds us of the continued growth of the commonwealth, which is playing a great part in the world in maintaining freedom and peace. The strengthening of the commonwealth is a primary objective of our government.
Several items, particularly those relating to old age pensions, aid for our Canadian industries and university assistance, were particularly commendable in the speech from the throne. As member of parliament in a riding which is strongly industrial I was happy to see four proposals which should assist in no small way toward helping industries to develop, and employment to increase. Aid to scientific research by industry and a national electric grid should be of tremendous assistance over the coming years. Critics might say these two moves will not bring aid to industries and cut employment fast


enough. I do not think they are really designed to do that. Instead, I am sure they are intelligent steps which, although they will not pay dividends for some time, will help to promote a steady industrial growth for all regions of Canada during coming decades.
The third item, broadening of the Small Business Loans Act, will give a further shot in the arm to our secondary industries at a time when our country is striving to move ahead in this phase of business activity.
Critics may again say that the measures outlined in the speech from the throne are not bold enough. However I say that the variety of moves, whether they are small or large, is an indication that our government has the welfare of many groups, individuals, and yes, of all Canadians at heart.
During the last four years many changes have been made in Waterloo North in regard to industry. The main street in the city of Waterloo with its new civic square, approval of new post offices in the twin cities of Kitchener and Waterloo, and of university buildings and other structures too numerous to mention, are some of the improvements that have taken place or are contemplated.
We will be asked to increase federal grants to universities and make suitable provision in those cases where alternative arrangements are made for supplementary provincial grants in lieu of federal grants. These increases will be welcomed by all universities across Canada, including universities in my riding of Waterloo North, the University of Waterloo, the Waterloo Lutheran University, and the University of St. Jerome's College, all of whose progress has been phenomenal. These institutions in the past have received financial aid from our government.
One of the most interesting developments during the last year in the North Waterloo riding has been the continued rapid development of the University of Waterloo. This institution was incorporated only five years ago. Since that time student enrolment has grown to over 1,200, with a faculty of 111 providing instruction in arts, science, engineering and graduate studies. The university is located on a 240-acre campus and now has three large science and engineering buildings in use, the last of which was constructed during the past year. As of this year the financial assets of the university total in excess of $9.5 million.
Construction of an arts building is now under way and is scheduled for completion in the fall of 1962 at a cost of $1,350,000. One of the interesting features of this building is that it includes a 500 seat amphitheatre patterned after the Stratford Shakespearian festival theatre, which suggests the possibility

of a close relationship between the University of Waterloo and Stratford, so essential in our modern world of today.
Also under construction at the present time, and scheduled for completion in 1962, are three teaching and residence buildings for federated and affiliated colleges. The university of St. Jerome's college, federated with the University of Waterloo, is building a residence to accommodate 100 men students. The Sisters of Notre Dame, associated with St. Jerome's college, are building a women's residence for 55 students. Renison college, an Anglican institution, is building a residence for 40 men and 40 women students and the total construction costs of these church colleges is in excess of $2,500,000.
The University of Waterloo has pioneered in the introduction of co-operative education in Canada. Co-operative education embodies a program in which the student alternates periods of on-campus study with equal periods spent in gaining practical experience in an industry, business firm, or service agency related to the student's university course.
The Waterloo Lutheran University, like others, has made tremendous strides during the last few years. This university, which celebrated its fiftieth anniversary last year, can look back over the past five decades with pride. Affiliated with the University of Western Ontario from 1925 to 1960, it is now an independent degree-granting university, and there has been tremendous growth on the campus since it became an independent degree-granting institution in 1959. I was pleased to be one of the speakers in December at the dedication of the new women's residence and the laying of the cornerstone for two more new buildings, the university theatre auditorium and the students' union. Also included in this expansion program are a men's residence and a dining hall, the former due to be constructed this year, as the final stage of a $1,500,000 expansion program. Enrolment has reached a total figure of 1,220 for the academic year 1961-62, which is an increase of 50 per cent over 1960-61.
The two distinct units controlled by this university are Waterloo University College and Waterloo Lutheran Seminary. The seminary is a sister institution to Waterloo University College. Its purpose is to educate young men for the ministry. Its graduates serve in seven provinces, the United States, India and South America. The federal Department of Labour recently approved additions to Eastwood collegiate in Kitchener, Waterloo collegiate in Waterloo, and the Elmira district high school for vocational and technical training. My riding of Waterloo North, with its many public schools, separate
The Address-Mr. Weichel schools, collegiates, colleges and universities will present many fine educational opportunities to our youth.
Over the past four years our government has amended the Pension Act on many occasions. These amendments include increases to disabled veterans and their dependants, war veterans allowance, Veterans' Land Act improvements, and other important changes.
It is gratifying to know that we will be asked to approve an amendment to the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act to authorize the payment of allowances under specified conditions to merchant seamen, firefighters, foresters, members of the voluntary aid detachments and certain other civilians whose war service overseas has been recognized in other respects. Other amending bills will bring about increased allowances and other improvements under the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act, and an extension of the qualifying period under the War Service Grants Act, Veterans Insurance Act and Veterans' Land Act. I am sure that every veteran in Canada and the citizens of this country will appreciate the approval of such amendments. As long as one veteran or his dependant is in need of assistance, this government will gladly meet this obligation.
One point that I have raised in the house on several occasions and which has given others and myself much concern is the qualification respecting the continuation of the allowance after death of a pensioner in receipt of a pension of less than 50 per cent. The present legislation provides that in the case of those in receipt of a pension of less than 50 per cent at the time of death and whose death is not established as due to pensionable disabilities, no pension or allowance is payable.
A great many widows have brought this to my attention and to the attention of other hon. members. I hope that the present legislation can be amended at some future date in order that we may improve the financial circumstances of these widows.
It is most satisfying to know that this session the government will propose important measures in the field of social welfare. What could be more important than assisting our senior citizens and looking after those who come under the Old Age Assistance Act, blind people, and those who are disabled? Our government has always been intensely interested in the welfare of these citizens and these improvements in the field of social welfare will be deeply appreciated by all concerned.
Recently our government passed a bill providing $5 million for encouraging our youth

The Address-Mr. Weichel in fitness and amateur sport. Representatives have now been chosen to sit on this council and should in the near future be able to carry out their important tasks. I hoped that someone would be selected from western Ontario, because this is one of the hotbeds of interest in fitness and amateur sports in Canada. Canada is fortunate in having so many outstanding sportsmen. Although only a limited number can be selected for the council at this time, I am sure others will be ready to assist this program which is so essential to the welfare of our youth. Incidentally, I might mention that this week is minor league hockey week in Canada and 200,000 boys will participate in this great game.
I should like to say a few words regarding agriculture in Waterloo county and the province of Ontario. Before doing so I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), for the success he has achieved in finding markets for grain, which has helped a great deal to reduce surplus stocks. Our government should also be commended for the proposed legislation mentioned in the speech from the throne. This should be of great assistance to the farmers of Canada, especially those in the prairie provinces.
We in Ontario, as well as people in other provinces, were disturbed to hear of the losses sustained by the prairie farmers during the 1961 drought. However, we are being asked to provide assistance by means of acreage payments to those who have been affected. As one who represents an Ontario riding, Waterloo North, I should like to say that this province ranks first among Canadian provinces in agricultural production and has for many years had the highest annual farm cash income of any province. It has one of the most diverse farming areas of any single administrative unit in North America.
It may be interesting to know that of the 1.5 million estimated rural population of Ontario, one third live on farms. The size of most farms is between 50 and 100 acres, but there are some 23,000 farms of 200 acres or more. The average size is 140 acres, Which is much smaller than the average prairie farm.
Livestock is the foundation of the agricultural economy of Ontario. In my riding dairy farming comes first in agricultural production, followed by hogs and beef feeding. Sheep used to be a familiar sight on many Ontario farms and it is certain that the new inducements our government is offering in the way of transportation of breeding ewes from the west, premiums on good lamb carcasses and price support for wool, are going to make farmers take another look at this line of livestock. There is a great deal of good land for sheep farming in the
[Mr. Weichel.1
province of Ontario. I understand that under the transportation assistance program for sheep which was announced recently by the Minister of Agriculture some 6,000 western range ewes were moved into Ontario last fall.
I now wish to say a few words about our younger folk. It is heartening to note that 4-H and junior farmers organizations are strong movements in the province of Ontario. There is no doubt that the cultivation of youth in the cause of our primary industry will bring the most suitable people into agriculture with the awareness of the need for good breeding and management practices already instilled into them.
Members of the 4-H organization contributed the facts and figures for a recent farm safety survey. This was a valuable type of service which we all hope will bring a reduction in the number of injuries and the amount of damage caused by carelessness at work on the farm. I understand that the federal Department of Agriculture contributed something in excess of $100,000 toward 4-H activities last year.
I should like to mention one further point. Ontario's poultry industry is one of the most remarkable developments in agriculture in this country. The production of chicken and turkey meat has multiplied several times in the last decade, and egg production has gone up by more than 1 million cases. Some of these products are beginning to be better known in the markets of Europe. The application of efficient management, breeding and feeding principles-for which federal research takes some credit-are among the reasons for the spectacular success of these industries.
I come from a community which is one of the largest cosmopolitan centres in Canada, and I think that old and new Canadians were deeply impressed when they learned that for the first time a bill of rights had become a reality under the leadership of our Prime Minister.
This bill, which is well known to Canadians, provides for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Our Prime Minister has through the years urged that such a bill be enacted. His untiring efforts in bringing about this bill should be an inspiration to all our people. The stand of our Prime Minister against racial discrimination at the commonwealth prime ministers' meeting in London bears living testimony to the principles for which he stands.
Since this bill was enacted I have heard people from all walks of life express their views with these words: "It is great to be a Canadian". Others have asked "What is a Canadian?" To this question may I express my observations in this way? We are citizens

of Canada, either by birth or by adoption and naturalization. We are citizens of the commonwealth. Our skins may be brown, yellow, black or white, but we are Canadians. Our names may be Poloski, Fraser, Wong, Spermanti, Dubois, Schmidt, Weichel or Jones. Our forefathers may have come from Glasgow, Prague, Tokyo; from Dublin, London, Paris, Rotterdam, Berlin, Madrid, or from countries such as Poland, Italy, the Ukraine or Israel. We may be labourer, student, businessman, member of parliament, news reporter, doctor, lawyer or machinist. Whatever we are, whatever our occupation, whatever our background, if we accept Canada as our country and with it the democratic way of life, we are Canadians.
We have the right to speak freely, to worship freely; but with these rights, we must learn our duties-to speak wisely, to worship wisely, to choose our leaders wisely. We inherit two great cultures, the Anglo-Saxon and the French, and more than 30 others as well. We are creating out of these a new and growing Canadian culture. At times we may whine when things go wrong, be unfair in our criticisms, forget to help the other fellow when in need, be unappreciative of some of our blessings. However, we finally realize that it is great to be a Canadian.
As we old and new Canadians travel along life's pathway together may we unite in one great effort for the progress of our country and the peace and welfare of all nations in the world. Perhaps I can close with these words as written by Kipling, words so often expressed during world war I:
It ain't the individual nor the army as a whole. But the everlasting teamwork of every blooming soul.

However, I said there was a fundamental difference between the New Democratic party and the others. In view of the fact speakers before me on the other side of the house have insisted on bringing up this matter, I 26207-1-12J
The Address-Mr. Winch think the fundamental difference should be made clear in this forum. Very briefly, in order that I shall not be misunderstood, may I say that it is our contention that every man and woman must learn that his welfare is to be found in the welfare of the whole community. This can only be learned through sharing social responsibility, and methods which do not vitalize and broaden social action shape results that are undemocratic. I have no hesitation in saying that the objective of the New Democratic party, the objective of those of us who sit here, cannot be handed to the people; that is why we do not make promises. Our objectives will arrive and endure when the people find an opportunity to accept and appreciate social responsibility.
We realize in this corner that we are in a social revolution today. We are not concerned about any revolution that may come tomorrow or one which is around the corner. Our concept of society, Mr. Speaker, our concept of Canada, is that natural forces compel change, growth and progress. We desire to remove, through democratic action, the existing restraints upon natural social change. I can say that basically and fundamentally the motivation behind this group speaking in the House of Commons is to use the instrument of political democracy, the parliament of Canada, in order to build an economic democracy which will provide not only greater economic efficiency but the greatest happiness to the greatest number.
We realize that Liberals, Conservatives and Socreds do not like the thought of revolutionary change. They do not like anything which will endanger the maintenance of their beloved system of free enterprise, business as usual and the devil take the hindmost. However, whether the Liberals and Conservatives like it or not, they are facing change. Progress and real democracy demand that we replace monopolistic enterprise by democratic socialism. We believe that this is something that could and should be done by common sense, conscious, deliberate methods and not through being the victim of blind processes, as unfortunately is the case far too often when governments move only when ultimately they are compelled to do so by circumstances or by public opinion built up for them by the New Democratic party.
We have always stated-and I wish to reiterate it-that it is the responsibility of all of us to emphasize that the ultimate goals of a real society in Canada, a society of personal and collective security and permanent peace, must be achieved by utilizing the political instrument for its supreme task of enabling this nation to meet the challenging times.

We are undoubtedly facing challenging times, Mr. Speaker, I know that if anybody dares to criticize the government or their party, their actions or their statements, we hear from the Conservative side of the house a great deal to the effect that we are doing a disservice to Canada and that we are bringing Canada into disrepute. When they say this they are completely ignoring the duties and responsibilities of members of parliament and are showing their own callousness and ineptitude. It is therefore necessary for them to bring out the blindfold in order to hide their own failures and shortcomings.
We live in an age of anxiety. We have anxiety in Canada domestically as to individual economic security and anxiety as to whether we are to have peace or war. It is the responsibility of all of us in this House of Commons to recognize that fact, to face up to and confront the problems and to see what we can do about them.
We hear a great deal about the national production and increases in employment. That is all to the good. We are happy about it. However, Mr. Speaker, statistics do not fill the bellies and pay the rent of those who are out of work; and I may say that there are many people who are out of work in my own province of British Columbia. According to the latest figures we have the second highest ratio of unemployment in Canada. Some people are losing their homes and their furniture-they are even losing their morale-because of the failure of this government to solve the problem they told us they were going to solve in 1958. I wish to say this, Mr. Speaker, you can use all the statistics you wish to use, but what the unemployed Canadian workers want are jobs and not statistics gumbo. I say that something is wrong in this country of Canada and with the government of Canada, when, at a time when there are slums to be cleared, homes to be built, roads to be built, hospitals and universities to be built, new resources to be opened up, we have existing conditions and unemployment.
I know the answer comes back, "Where is the money coming from?" I have enough pride in Canada and in Canadians to believe that if we can find, as we did, $44 billion in order to wage two world wars and maintain the Department of National Defence, we can find the money with which to put our unemployed to work. I am certain that the people of Canada will respond to an invitation to make an investment in prosperity and peace just as fully as, if not more fully, than they will respond to an invitation to make an investment in order to win a war.


If the government have not that confidence, they have no business to be in the seats of administration in this country.
I have heard it said so often that these things are impossible. I heard that word "impossible" from a government speaker just the other night when we had a debate at Carleton University. It should be understood that the word "impossible" means only one thing, namely those things that have not been done yet. Let us start doing some of the things that are long overdue, not only in the domestic field of endeavour but also in the international field.
May I say that one of the greatest heartbreaks of my life is to see the way in which this government has brought Canada into international disrepute and made her the laughingstock of the nations of the world.

subtopic: CANADA-U.K.  COMMUNIQUE ON EUROPEAN TRADE DEVELOPMENTS

speechtext:
Ottawa, January 4, 1962
Canadian ministers and Mr. Edward Heath, Lord Privy Seal in the British government, have concluded two days of useful and constructive talks concerning European trading developments. The Canadian ministers taking part in the meeting were Hon. Donald M. Fleming, Minister of Finance, chairman, Hon. Howard Green, Secretary of State for External Affairs, Hon. George Hees, Minister of Trade and Commerce, Hon. Alvin Hamilton, Minister of Agriculture.
During the discussions Mr. Heath informed Canadian ministers of current developments in Britain's negotiations with the European economic community. He stressed the efforts being made by the United Kingdom to safeguard the essential trade interests of Canada and other commonwealth countries. Canadian ministers welcomed his statement and emphasized the extent and importance of Canadian interests in the British market. They indicated that they would provide the British government with complete information on all aspects of Canadian trade interests relevant to the negotiations in Brussels. The ministers reaffirmed that full consultation and co-operation would be maintained between the two governments throughout the negotiations in Brussels and that the means to this end would be adapted as circumstances might require.
There was complete agreement on the great value of commonwealth trade links and the need to maintain them. It was also agreed that when the talks with the European economic community are further advanced it may be desirable to examine what additional arrangements for consultation with commonwealth countries are necessary.
Mr. Heath and the Canadian ministers noted the conclusions of the recent meeting of trade ministers arranged by the GATT in Geneva concerning future tariff negotiations, trade in agricultural products, and obstacles to the trade of the less developed countries. They welcomed the recent reaffirmation by the ministerial council of the organization for economic co-operation and development of the objective of expanding world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis. They stressed the importance they
attach to further progress in the reduction of tariffs and other barriers to world trade.
Ottawa, January 13, 1962

maintopic: SEVENTH MEETING OP JOINT CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE ON TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS

speechtext:
The seventh meeting of the joint Canada-United States committee on trade and economic affairs was held in Ottawa, January 12 and 13, 1962, under the chairmanship of Hon. Donald M. Fleming, Minister of Finance.
2.	The United States was represented at the meeting by Hon. C. Douglas Dillon, Secretary of the Treasury; Hon. Stewart Udall, Secretary of the Interior; Hon. Orville L. Freeman, Secretary of Agriculture; Hon. Luther H. Hodges, Secretary of Commerce; and Hon. George W. Ball, undersecretary of state. The United States delegation also included Mr. Livingston T. Merchant, United States ambassador to Canada.
3.	Canada was represented by Hon. Howard Green, Secretary of State for External Affairs; Hon. Donald M. Fleming, Minister of Finance; Hon. George Hees, Minister of Trade and Commerce; and Hon. Alvin Hamilton, Minister of Agriculture. The Canadian delegation included the Canadian ambassador to the United States, Mr. A. D. P. Heeney.
4.	The committee noted the improvement in the level of economic activity in both countries since the previous meeting in Washington in March, 1961. They agreed on the importance of achieving sustained economic growth in accordance with the resolution adopted at the first ministerial meeting of the OECD on November 17. Measures for the expansion of world trade would be essential to the achievement of these aims.
5.	Canadian ministers reiterated their support for the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis, and Canada's readiness to play a constructive role in the promotion of freer world trade. United States members welcomed this statement and pointed out that the United States had consistently supported these objectives for many years. The committee recognized the importance of the recent decision at the GATT ministerial meeting to explore new arrangements for the multilateral reduction of trade barriers and for moving toward freer trade. The

United States members emphasized that the new trade legislation being sought at this session of congress is intended to contribute substantially to this objective.
6.	The United States members explained the general nature and purposes of the trade expansion program which the United States administration will be submitting to congress, which, if approved, would enable the United States to make a greater contribution to the growth of international trade on a multilateral basis, and in this way contribute substantially to the strength and prosperity of the free world.
7.	The committee examined the problems inhibiting international trade in agricultural commodities and underlined the importance of securing international agreement on measures which would provide adequate access to world markets for agricultural producers. They agreed that such measures should take full account of the comparative advantage of production in agricultural commodities among different countries. United States and Canadian ministers expressed the hope that coming international discussions would effectively contribute to the freeing and expansion of international trade in agricultural products.
8.	The committee noted the current negotiations between Britain and the European economic community and the widespread consequences which British entry into the E.E.C. would have for the rest of the world. The
committee recognized the great importance of the commonwealth as a unique association of free nations bridging five continents and the constructive contribution which it was making to world peace and stability.
9.	Canadian ministers emphasized that the commonwealth trade links, including the exchange of preferences and the historic right of free entry into the United Kingdom market, were an essential cohesive element in the commonwealth association. They stressed the importance the Canadian government attached to Britain's efforts in their negotiations with the E.E.C. to safeguard the trade interests of Canada and other commonwealth countries.
10.	The committee recalled the constructive conclusions reached at the recent ministerial meeting of the GATT concerning the trade of the less developed countries. They reaffirmed that it was the continuing policy of both countries to assist the efforts of those countries to expand their trade and improve their standards of living.
11.	The committee recognized that direct exchanges of views at the cabinet level are useful in helping to maintain soundly based and effective economic co-operation between Canada and the United States. Such understanding and co-operation will be all the more necessary in the years ahead if each country is to play its part in a changing world with a full recognition of the essential interests and aspirations of the other.
Thursday. January 25, 1962
